questions.question: A user's phone shows 5G in the status bar at home but only LTE in a rural area. Both allow calls and browsing. What does the change indicate?
options: The phone has fallen back to the older cellular network generation available in that location
The phone's SIM card has been deactivated
The phone has switched to Wi-Fi calling
The phone's cellular radio has failed
questions.explanation: Cellular phones hold radios for several generations and use the fastest one the nearest tower offers. 5G coverage is concentrated in cities, so a phone that shows 5G at home and LTE (4G) in the countryside is behaving correctly and will still make calls and pass data, just at lower peak speeds. A deactivated SIM would show no service, Wi-Fi calling shows its own indicator, and a failed radio would leave the phone with no cellular signal at all.

distractor_analysis.1: A deactivated SIM produces no service rather than a slower generation.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi calling has its own status indicator and needs a Wi-Fi network.
distractor_analysis.3: A failed radio shows no signal, not LTE.

questions.question: A phone has a strong Wi-Fi signal but web pages will not load, while the same pages load fine on cellular data. What should the technician check first?
options: Whether the Wi-Fi network has internet access or requires a captive portal sign-in
Whether the phone's SIM card is seated
Whether Bluetooth is enabled
Whether the phone needs a new battery
questions.explanation: Signal strength only shows that the phone is associated with the access point. A hotel, airport or guest network usually demands a captive-portal login before it forwards traffic, and a home router can lose its upstream connection while still broadcasting a strong Wi-Fi signal. Opening a browser to trigger the portal, or checking the router's internet light, resolves most cases. The SIM is proven fine by working cellular data, and Bluetooth and the battery are unrelated.

distractor_analysis.1: Cellular data works, so the SIM is seated and active.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth has no role in Wi-Fi internet access.
distractor_analysis.3: Battery state does not block web traffic.

questions.question: A traveller wants to stop a phone using any radio during a flight but still listen to downloaded music with wired headphones. Which setting achieves this?
options: Airplane mode
Do Not Disturb
Low power mode
Data roaming off
questions.explanation: Airplane mode disables the cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios in one switch while leaving the rest of the phone usable, so offline music, downloaded films and local apps continue to work. On most phones Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can be re-enabled individually while airplane mode stays on, which is how in-flight Wi-Fi and wireless earbuds are used. Do Not Disturb only silences notifications, low power mode throttles performance, and data roaming controls only cellular data abroad.

distractor_analysis.1: Do Not Disturb leaves every radio on.
distractor_analysis.2: Low power mode saves battery but does not disable radios.
distractor_analysis.3: Data roaming is a cellular billing control, not a radio switch.

questions.question: A user returns from abroad to a very large phone bill. The phone was used for maps and email throughout the trip. Which setting would have prevented the charges?
options: Turning off data roaming, or buying a travel data plan before departure
Turning off Bluetooth
Enabling Do Not Disturb
Lowering the screen brightness
questions.explanation: Roaming means the phone attaches to a foreign carrier's network, and data used there is billed at that carrier's rates unless the home plan includes roaming. Disabling data roaming makes the phone use only Wi-Fi for data abroad, and a travel plan or local SIM caps the cost. Technicians supporting travelling staff should set expectations before the trip. Bluetooth, notification settings and brightness have no effect on cellular data charges.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth uses no cellular data.
distractor_analysis.2: Do Not Disturb hides alerts but apps still sync in the background.
distractor_analysis.3: Brightness affects battery, not billing.

questions.question: A user needs to work on a laptop in a park with no Wi-Fi. The phone has a good cellular signal. What is the quickest way to get the laptop online?
options: Enable the phone's Wi-Fi hotspot and join the laptop to it
Pair the laptop and phone over NFC
Plug the phone into the laptop's HDMI port
Enable airplane mode on the phone
questions.explanation: A hotspot turns the phone into a small Wi-Fi access point that shares its cellular data connection. The laptop joins it like any other network, using the password shown on the phone. Technicians should remind users that hotspot use counts against the phone plan's data allowance, drains the battery quickly, and that USB tethering is an alternative that charges the phone at the same time. NFC and HDMI do not carry internet, and airplane mode would switch the cellular radio off.

distractor_analysis.1: NFC exchanges tiny amounts of data at very short range.
distractor_analysis.2: HDMI carries video, not network traffic.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode disables the very radio that provides the data.

questions.question: A phone's location in a mapping app is accurate outdoors but jumps around or is unavailable inside a large building. Why?
options: GPS needs a clear view of satellites, and indoors the phone falls back to less precise Wi-Fi and cellular positioning
The phone's SIM card cannot be read indoors
Mapping apps only work over Wi-Fi
The phone's compass is broken
questions.explanation: Satellite positioning depends on receiving weak signals from several satellites at once, and roofs and floors block them. Indoors the phone estimates location from known Wi-Fi access points and cell towers, which is accurate to tens or hundreds of metres rather than a few metres, hence the jumping. This is normal behaviour, not a fault. The SIM is unaffected by buildings, mapping works over any data connection, and the compass gives heading rather than position.

distractor_analysis.1: SIM operation does not depend on the phone's surroundings.
distractor_analysis.2: Maps work over cellular data as well as Wi-Fi.
distractor_analysis.3: A compass fault would affect the direction arrow, not the position.

questions.question: Which technology allows a phone to determine its position using signals from orbiting satellites?
options: GPS and other global navigation satellite systems
NFC
Bluetooth
Cellular triangulation
questions.explanation: Phones include a receiver for GPS and usually for other constellations such as Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou, which are collectively called global navigation satellite systems. The receiver measures the time of arrival of signals from at least four satellites to compute a position, typically within a few metres outdoors. The receiver is passive and works without a data plan, although maps need data to download. Cellular triangulation is a fallback estimate, and NFC and Bluetooth are short-range links.

distractor_analysis.1: NFC operates over centimetres and has no positioning role.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth beacons can assist indoors but do not provide global positioning.
distractor_analysis.3: Cell triangulation is a coarse fallback, not the satellite technology asked about.

questions.question: A company issues phones and wants to enforce a passcode, push corporate Wi-Fi settings and remotely wipe a lost device. Which type of system provides these controls?
options: Mobile device management (MDM)
A mobile hotspot
A cloud photo backup service
A Bluetooth beacon network
questions.explanation: MDM platforms enrol phones and tablets so an administrator can push configuration profiles, require a passcode and encryption, install or block apps, and wipe or lock a device that is lost. Devices are enrolled either automatically through the vendor's business programme or manually with an enrolment app or profile. MDM is the foundation of corporate mobile support. Hotspots, photo backup and beacons solve entirely different problems.

distractor_analysis.1: A hotspot shares a data connection.
distractor_analysis.2: Photo backup protects pictures, not device policy.
distractor_analysis.3: Beacons provide indoor location, not management.

questions.question: An employee wants to use a personal phone for work email. The company requires that corporate data can be removed without touching personal photos and messages. Which MDM approach satisfies this?
options: A bring-your-own-device policy using a managed work profile or container with selective wipe
Full device enrolment with mandatory factory reset on departure
Disabling the phone's camera
Requiring the phone to stay on the office Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: Modern MDM separates work and personal data on a personal device. Android creates a work profile and iOS uses managed apps and accounts, so corporate email, contacts and files live in a container that the administrator controls. When the employee leaves, a selective wipe removes only that container and leaves personal content untouched. A full factory reset would violate the requirement, and camera or network restrictions do not address data separation.

distractor_analysis.1: A factory reset destroys the employee's personal data.
distractor_analysis.2: Disabling the camera is a policy control unrelated to data separation.
distractor_analysis.3: Network restrictions do not partition data on the device.

questions.question: A sales team's phones must sign in to corporate email with a certificate instead of a password, and the certificate must be installed on every phone without user involvement. Which mechanism does this?
options: A configuration profile pushed by the MDM containing the account settings and certificate
Emailing each user a PDF with instructions
Enabling Bluetooth file sharing
Setting the phones to airplane mode during setup
questions.explanation: MDM configuration profiles are signed bundles of settings: mail accounts, Wi-Fi networks, VPN definitions, certificates and restrictions. When pushed to an enrolled phone, the settings apply silently, so every device gets the same account and certificate with no user typing. This is how enterprises deploy certificate-based authentication at scale. Manual instructions do not scale and invite errors, Bluetooth sharing is insecure for credentials, and airplane mode blocks the push.

distractor_analysis.1: Manual steps on hundreds of phones are slow and error-prone.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth sharing is not a management channel.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode disconnects the phone from the MDM server.

questions.question: A user configures a corporate email account on a phone using only an email address and password, and the phone finds the server settings automatically. Which feature made this possible?
options: Autodiscover, which looks up the mail server configuration from the domain
Bluetooth pairing with the mail server
A hotspot connection
GPS location services
questions.explanation: Modern mail systems such as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace publish their server details so a client can look them up from the domain part of the address. The phone queries the autodiscover record, retrieves the server names, ports and security settings, and completes the account with just the credentials. If autodiscover is missing the user must enter incoming and outgoing server settings manually, which is where support calls come from.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth has no role in email configuration.
distractor_analysis.2: A hotspot provides connectivity but not server settings.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services do not discover mail servers.

questions.question: A user sets up a personal email account on a phone and finds that deleting a message on the phone does not remove it from the webmail inbox. Which protocol is the phone most likely using?
options: POP3, which downloads messages and does not keep the mailbox in sync
IMAP, which keeps every client synchronised with the server
Exchange ActiveSync
SMTP
questions.explanation: POP3 pulls copies of messages to the device and, depending on settings, leaves the originals on the server, so actions on one device are not reflected anywhere else. IMAP and Exchange ActiveSync keep the mailbox on the server and synchronise every folder and read or delete state to all clients, which is the behaviour users expect today. Switching the account to IMAP fixes the complaint. SMTP only sends mail and never affects the inbox.

distractor_analysis.1: IMAP would have deleted the message everywhere.
distractor_analysis.2: ActiveSync synchronises state across devices in the same way as IMAP.
distractor_analysis.3: SMTP is the outgoing protocol and does not manage the inbox.

questions.question: A user must manually configure a mail account on a phone. The provider says incoming mail uses IMAP over SSL and outgoing uses SMTP with STARTTLS. Which port pair is correct?
options: Incoming 993, outgoing 587
Incoming 110, outgoing 25
Incoming 143, outgoing 465
Incoming 995, outgoing 80
questions.explanation: IMAP over an implicit SSL/TLS connection listens on TCP 993, and the modern client submission port for SMTP, which starts unencrypted and upgrades with STARTTLS, is TCP 587. Port 110 is plain POP3 and 25 is server-to-server relay that most providers block for clients. Port 143 is unencrypted IMAP, 465 is SMTP over implicit TLS rather than STARTTLS, and 995 is POP3 over SSL with 80 being HTTP. Matching the port to the encryption method is what makes the account connect.

distractor_analysis.1: 110 and 25 are unencrypted POP3 and relay SMTP.
distractor_analysis.2: 143 is IMAP without encryption and 465 is implicit TLS rather than STARTTLS.
distractor_analysis.3: 995 is secure POP3 and 80 is web traffic.

questions.question: A user replaced a lost phone and, after signing in to the same account, found contacts, calendar and photos restored automatically. Which feature made this happen?
options: Cloud synchronisation and backup tied to the user's account
Bluetooth transfer from the old phone
A SIM card swap
An MDM remote wipe
questions.explanation: Both major platforms continuously synchronise contacts, calendars, notes and settings to the account in the cloud, and take periodic full backups over Wi-Fi. Signing in on a new device pulls that data back down. Technicians should confirm backup is enabled and has run recently before any repair or replacement. The old phone was lost, so no local transfer was possible; a SIM only carries the subscriber identity, and a wipe removes data rather than restoring it.

distractor_analysis.1: The old phone was lost, so it could not be the source.
distractor_analysis.2: A SIM does not store contacts or photos in modern use.
distractor_analysis.3: A remote wipe erases a device.

questions.question: A user complains that photos taken on the phone do not appear on the laptop even though both use the same cloud account. The phone has been on cellular data all day. What is the most likely reason?
options: Photo synchronisation is set to upload over Wi-Fi only and the phone has not been on Wi-Fi
The laptop needs a SIM card
The photos are too high resolution to sync
Bluetooth is disabled on the laptop
questions.explanation: Cloud photo services default to uploading over Wi-Fi to protect the user's cellular allowance, so pictures taken away from Wi-Fi queue up until the phone returns to a wireless network. The user can either join Wi-Fi or enable cellular upload in the app settings. Laptops do not need SIMs to reach cloud services, resolution does not block sync, and Bluetooth plays no part in cloud synchronisation.

distractor_analysis.1: The laptop reaches the cloud over its own internet connection.
distractor_analysis.2: Cloud services accept full-resolution photos.
distractor_analysis.3: Cloud sync runs over the internet, not Bluetooth.

questions.question: A phone's storage is full and the user is told that enabling cloud photo storage will help. How does that feature typically free space?
options: Full-resolution originals are kept in the cloud and the phone keeps smaller optimised versions
Photos are compressed to black and white
Photos are moved to the SIM card
The phone deletes all photos older than a week
questions.explanation: Optimised storage keeps the original files safely in the account and replaces local copies with device-sized versions, downloading the original on demand when the user opens or edits a picture. This can free many gigabytes without losing anything. Users should understand that the originals now depend on the account and that a full-resolution download needs connectivity. Colour is unchanged, SIMs hold no photos, and nothing is deleted from the account.

distractor_analysis.1: Optimised versions are full colour, just smaller.
distractor_analysis.2: SIM cards hold kilobytes of subscriber data, not photos.
distractor_analysis.3: Photos remain in the cloud indefinitely.

questions.question: An administrator needs to locate a company tablet that was left in a taxi and then erase it if it cannot be recovered. Which capability of the management platform does this rely on?
options: Remote locate and remote wipe on an enrolled device
Bluetooth tethering
Configuration profile for Wi-Fi
App store restrictions
questions.explanation: MDM and the platform vendors' own services can report an enrolled device's last known location, play a sound, lock it with a message, and finally wipe it. The wipe command executes as soon as the device next connects to any network, which is why the device should be locked first rather than wiped immediately if there is a chance of recovery. Tethering, Wi-Fi profiles and app restrictions are unrelated to finding or erasing a lost device.

distractor_analysis.1: Tethering shares data; it does not locate anything.
distractor_analysis.2: A Wi-Fi profile configures networks, not device recovery.
distractor_analysis.3: App restrictions control what can be installed.

questions.question: A company wants every corporate phone to require two-factor authentication for its email app and to block the app from copying text into personal apps. Which category of MDM control handles the copy restriction?
options: Mobile application management (MAM) or app protection policies
Wi-Fi configuration profiles
Remote wipe
Location services
questions.explanation: Application-level management applies policy inside managed apps: requiring a PIN or biometric to open the app, blocking cut and paste to unmanaged apps, preventing saving to personal storage and encrypting app data. It works alongside device enrolment and is the only way to enforce these controls on a personal device. Wi-Fi profiles, remote wipe and location are device-level features that do not govern data movement between apps.

distractor_analysis.1: Wi-Fi profiles push network settings.
distractor_analysis.2: Remote wipe erases; it does not govern day-to-day data flow.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services report position and do not control clipboard use.

questions.question: A user cannot enrol a new phone in the company's MDM. The enrolment app reports that the device is not eligible. The phone was bought second-hand. What is the most likely cause?
options: The device is still registered to the previous owner's account or management, an activation lock
The phone's Bluetooth is off
The phone has too much free storage
The user has not set a wallpaper
questions.explanation: Both platforms tie a device to the account or organisation that last activated it. A second-hand phone whose previous owner did not sign out and remove it stays locked to that owner, and a phone previously enrolled by another company stays in that company's management programme. Enrolment is refused until the previous party releases it. This is also why corporate procurement prefers devices bought through channels that register them directly to the company.

distractor_analysis.1: Enrolment works over Wi-Fi or cellular and does not need Bluetooth.
distractor_analysis.2: Free storage is never a barrier to enrolment.
distractor_analysis.3: Wallpaper is cosmetic.

questions.question: A user asks what the tiny removable card in the phone's side tray is for. What is the correct answer?
options: It is the SIM, which identifies the subscriber to the carrier's network
It stores all the user's photos
It holds the phone's operating system
It is the Bluetooth antenna
questions.explanation: The subscriber identity module carries the account identity and authentication key that let the carrier recognise the phone on its network. Moving the SIM to another unlocked phone moves the number and plan with it. Many current phones also or only support an eSIM, a built-in chip provisioned electronically by the carrier, which is why some models have no tray. Photos and the operating system live in the phone's own flash storage, and the antennas are internal to the chassis.

distractor_analysis.1: Photos are stored in the phone's internal storage or the cloud.
distractor_analysis.2: The operating system is on internal flash, not a removable card.
distractor_analysis.3: Antennas are built into the frame or display assembly.

questions.question: A traveller wants to use a local carrier's data plan abroad without removing the home SIM. The phone supports eSIM. What should the technician recommend?
options: Add the local carrier's eSIM profile alongside the physical SIM and select it for data
Cut the home SIM down to fit a second tray
Enable Bluetooth tethering to a local phone
Use airplane mode for the whole trip
questions.explanation: An eSIM is a programmable chip in the phone that stores one or more carrier profiles. A traveller can buy a local or travel data plan online, scan a QR code to add the profile, and set that line for data while keeping the home number active for calls and texts. This avoids roaming charges and the risk of losing a tiny plastic card. Cutting SIMs risks damage, tethering depends on someone else's phone, and airplane mode disconnects everything.

distractor_analysis.1: Cutting a SIM can destroy it and most phones have one tray.
distractor_analysis.2: Tethering to another person's phone is not a plan of one's own.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode removes connectivity rather than adding a plan.

questions.question: A phone shows full cellular bars but calls fail and data is very slow in a packed stadium. What is the most likely cause?
options: The local cell is congested by the number of users, so capacity rather than signal is the limit
The SIM has expired
The phone's antenna is damaged
Airplane mode is on
questions.explanation: Signal bars measure how strongly the phone hears the tower, not how much capacity the tower has left. In a crowd tens of thousands of phones share one cell, and the radio channels and backhaul saturate, so calls fail to set up and data crawls despite excellent signal. Carriers add temporary cells at big events for this reason. An expired SIM shows no service everywhere, a damaged antenna shows weak bars, and airplane mode shows no bars at all.

distractor_analysis.1: An expired SIM fails everywhere, not only in the stadium.
distractor_analysis.2: Antenna damage reduces signal strength rather than leaving full bars.
distractor_analysis.3: Airplane mode removes the signal indicator entirely.

questions.question: A user in a building with poor cellular coverage still receives calls on the phone over the office Wi-Fi. Which feature is in use?
options: Wi-Fi calling
Bluetooth calling
NFC calling
Satellite calling
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi calling routes voice calls and texts over any internet connection to the carrier's core network, so the phone behaves as though it has cellular coverage even in a basement or a rural house. It must be enabled in the phone settings and supported by the carrier, and an emergency address is registered so emergency services can locate the caller. Bluetooth carries audio to a headset but not calls to the network, NFC is for taps, and satellite messaging on some phones is emergency text only.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth links the phone to accessories, not to the carrier.
distractor_analysis.2: NFC cannot carry a voice call.
distractor_analysis.3: Satellite features are for emergency messaging, not everyday calls.

questions.question: A phone's battery drains far faster than usual after the user moved to an office at the edge of cellular coverage. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The cellular radio is transmitting at maximum power to hold a weak signal
The phone's storage is nearly full
The screen protector is too thick
The user's contacts list is too long
questions.explanation: A phone continuously adjusts its transmit power to reach the tower. At the edge of coverage it runs the radio near full power and repeatedly searches for a better cell, and that is one of the biggest battery drains on any handset. Enabling Wi-Fi calling, so the phone can prefer the office Wi-Fi for voice and data, usually restores normal battery life. Storage, protectors and contacts have no effect on power consumption.

distractor_analysis.1: Full storage slows the phone but does not drain the battery.
distractor_analysis.2: A protector is passive glass or film.
distractor_analysis.3: Contact list size is trivial data with no power cost.

questions.question: A company wants to allow only approved apps on its warehouse scanners and prevent staff from opening anything else. Which MDM feature provides this?
options: Kiosk or single-app mode with an allow list of applications
Remote wipe
Wi-Fi calling
Cloud photo backup
questions.explanation: Dedicated-device or kiosk mode locks a handset to one app or a small allow list, hides the home screen and settings, and can prevent the device leaving the app even after a reboot. It is the standard configuration for scanners, point-of-sale tablets and public displays. Remote wipe is for lost devices, Wi-Fi calling is a voice feature, and photo backup is a consumer service; none of them restricts which apps run.

distractor_analysis.1: Remote wipe erases a device and does not control app use.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi calling is about voice over wireless networks.
distractor_analysis.3: Photo backup does not restrict applications.

questions.question: After enrolling in MDM, a user's phone shows a corporate Wi-Fi network as connected but a corporate intranet site is unreachable while public sites load. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The VPN profile pushed by the MDM has not connected or was not included, so internal resources are unreachable
The phone's SIM card is missing
The screen brightness is too low
The phone's storage is full
questions.explanation: Internal sites normally sit behind the corporate firewall and require a VPN or a per-app VPN tunnel that the MDM configures. If the VPN profile is missing, the certificate has not arrived, or the user has not authenticated to it, public internet works but intranet names fail. Checking the VPN status in settings and confirming the profile installed is the fix. SIM, brightness and storage have no bearing on reaching internal sites.

distractor_analysis.1: The phone is on Wi-Fi; cellular identity is irrelevant.
distractor_analysis.2: Brightness is a display setting.
distractor_analysis.3: Full storage does not block network destinations.

questions.question: A user's phone contacts are duplicated after adding a second account. What is the recommended first step?
options: Check which accounts are set to sync contacts and disable contact sync on the redundant account
Factory reset the phone
Remove the SIM card
Turn off Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: Each account on a phone can sync its own contacts, calendar and mail. When two accounts hold copies of the same people, the phone shows both sets. Turning off contact sync for one account, or using the contacts app's merge duplicates feature, cleans the list without losing data. A factory reset is far out of proportion, the SIM rarely stores contacts on modern phones, and Wi-Fi has nothing to do with which accounts sync.

distractor_analysis.1: A reset wipes the device for a settings problem.
distractor_analysis.2: Modern contacts live in accounts, not on the SIM.
distractor_analysis.3: Wi-Fi state does not change account sync settings.

questions.question: Before sending a phone for a screen repair, what should a technician ask the user to do to protect their data?
options: Confirm a current cloud or computer backup exists, then sign out of accounts or enable a passcode as policy requires
Remove the screen protector
Turn off Bluetooth
Delete all photos to save space
questions.explanation: A repair can end in a replaced or wiped device, so the essential protection is a verified backup taken to the cloud or a computer immediately beforehand. Many repair shops also require the activation lock to be disabled, which means signing out of the platform account, and corporate policy may instead require the passcode to stay on. Protectors and Bluetooth are irrelevant, and deleting photos destroys exactly what the backup is meant to preserve.

distractor_analysis.1: The protector has no bearing on data safety.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth state does not protect data.
distractor_analysis.3: Deleting photos is data loss, not protection.

questions.question: A user complains that a phone connects to a public Wi-Fi hotspot at a cafe automatically every visit, which the company security team has told staff to avoid. What setting resolves this?
options: Forget the network or disable auto-join for that network
Enable airplane mode permanently
Remove the SIM card
Increase the screen timeout
questions.explanation: Phones remember networks they have joined and rejoin them automatically. Forgetting the network removes the saved profile, and most phones also offer a per-network auto-join toggle so the network can be used deliberately but not automatically. MDM can go further and block unmanaged networks. Airplane mode would remove all connectivity, the SIM is unrelated to Wi-Fi, and screen timeout is a display setting.

distractor_analysis.1: Airplane mode disables cellular too, which is not wanted.
distractor_analysis.2: Wi-Fi does not depend on the SIM.
distractor_analysis.3: Screen timeout affects the display only.

questions.question: A corporate phone's email stopped syncing after the user changed their domain password on a laptop. Other apps work. What is the most likely fix?
options: Update the stored password for the mail account on the phone
Replace the SIM
Reset network settings
Turn off location services
questions.explanation: Mail clients store the account credential and present it on every sync. When the password changes elsewhere, the phone keeps offering the old one, the server rejects it and sync stops, sometimes silently or with a re-enter password prompt. Entering the new password in the account settings restores sync; repeated failures can also lock the account, so acting quickly matters. Network reset, SIM and location services are unrelated to a credential mismatch.

distractor_analysis.1: The SIM has nothing to do with email authentication.
distractor_analysis.2: Network settings are fine because other apps work.
distractor_analysis.3: Location services do not affect mail sync.

questions.question: A user has Bluetooth enabled and a Wi-Fi hotspot running on the phone at the same time and notices the hotspot is slow. Both radios share the same band. Which band is that?
options: 2.4 GHz
5 GHz
6 GHz
900 MHz
questions.explanation: Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz band, the same band used by 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so a phone acting as a hotspot on 2.4 GHz while streaming to Bluetooth earbuds is competing with itself, and microwave ovens and neighbours' networks add more interference. Switching the hotspot to 5 GHz, where the phone supports it, moves the Wi-Fi traffic out of the crowded band. 6 GHz is Wi-Fi 6E and 7 only, and 900 MHz is used by cellular and some IoT radios, not Bluetooth.

distractor_analysis.1: Bluetooth does not use 5 GHz.
distractor_analysis.2: 6 GHz is reserved for newer Wi-Fi standards.
distractor_analysis.3: 900 MHz is a cellular and IoT band, not Bluetooth.

questions.question: A phone is enrolled in MDM and the administrator has enforced a six-digit passcode and encryption. The user asks why encryption matters if there is already a passcode. What is the accurate answer?
options: Encryption protects the stored data if the storage is read directly, while the passcode only guards the normal user interface
Encryption makes the phone charge faster
Encryption is required for Bluetooth to work
Encryption removes the need for backups
questions.explanation: A passcode stops someone using the phone through its screen, but without encryption the flash storage could be read with forensic tools. Device encryption scrambles the storage with a key derived in part from the passcode and stored in secure hardware, so the data is unreadable without both. Modern phones encrypt by default, and MDM enforces it so the setting cannot be turned off. Encryption has no effect on charging or Bluetooth and does not replace backups.

distractor_analysis.1: Encryption is a security control with no effect on charging.
distractor_analysis.2: Bluetooth operates independently of storage encryption.
distractor_analysis.3: Encrypted data can still be lost; backups remain essential.

questions.question: A small business owner asks whether staff phones need MDM if they only use web email. Which benefit of MDM is still relevant?
options: Enforcing screen lock and encryption and being able to wipe a lost phone that holds cached company data
Making the phones charge faster
Providing GPS satellites
Increasing cellular signal strength
questions.explanation: Even a browser caches credentials, cookies and downloaded attachments, and staff inevitably store contacts and messages. MDM ensures every phone has a lock screen and encryption and gives the business a way to wipe a device that goes missing, which is the minimum most data protection rules expect. The other options are not things any management platform can do; charging, satellites and radio signal are physical matters.

distractor_analysis.1: Charging speed is hardware and charger dependent.
distractor_analysis.2: GPS satellites are operated by governments, not MDM vendors.
distractor_analysis.3: Signal strength depends on the carrier network.

questions.question: A user's phone shows a Wi-Fi symbol with an exclamation mark and apps report no connection, but the laptop on the same network is fine. Which step is most likely to resolve it?
options: Forget and rejoin the Wi-Fi network, or toggle Wi-Fi off and on, to obtain a fresh network address
Replace the phone's battery
Remove the screen protector
Change the ringtone
questions.explanation: The exclamation indicator means the phone is associated but has no working route to the internet, commonly because its DHCP lease failed or a stale address is in use. Rejoining the network forces a new address and DNS settings from the router. If every device were affected the router would be the suspect, but a working laptop points at the phone's own connection state. Battery, protector and ringtone have nothing to do with networking.

distractor_analysis.1: Battery condition does not affect IP addressing.
distractor_analysis.2: A protector is passive.
distractor_analysis.3: Ringtones are unrelated to connectivity.

questions.question: A technician is asked to explain the difference between synchronising a phone to the cloud and backing it up. Which statement is accurate?
options: Sync keeps live data such as contacts identical across devices, while a backup is a point-in-time copy used to restore a device
Sync and backup are the same operation
Backups only include photos
Sync only works over a cable
questions.explanation: Synchronisation continuously mirrors changing data, so deleting a contact on one device deletes it everywhere, which means sync alone cannot recover from a mistake. A backup captures the whole device at a moment, including app data and settings, and is what a replacement phone is restored from. Both are needed. Backups include far more than photos, and both sync and backup normally run over Wi-Fi.

distractor_analysis.1: They serve different purposes and behave differently on deletion.
distractor_analysis.2: Backups cover settings, app data, messages and more.
distractor_analysis.3: Sync is wireless by default.

questions.question: A company is deciding between issuing corporate phones and allowing personal phones for work. Which TWO statements about MDM are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: Corporate-owned devices can be fully managed, including complete wipe and strict restrictions
Personal devices are typically managed with a work profile or managed apps so only corporate data is controlled
MDM can only manage devices from one manufacturer
MDM requires every phone to be connected by USB to the administrator's computer
MDM cannot enforce a passcode
questions.explanation: Ownership determines the management model. A company-owned device can be supervised or fully managed, with every setting under administrative control and a full wipe available. A personal device is enrolled with a work profile or managed apps so the company controls only its own data and can remove just that. MDM platforms manage iOS, Android and often Windows and macOS together, they work entirely over the network, and enforcing passcodes is one of their basic functions.

distractor_analysis.2: Major MDM platforms manage several vendors' devices.
distractor_analysis.3: Enrolment and policy are delivered over the air.
distractor_analysis.4: Passcode enforcement is a core MDM capability.

questions.question: A user is about to travel internationally with a corporate phone. Which TWO actions should the technician recommend before departure? (Select TWO.)
options: Confirm the plan includes roaming or add a travel plan or local eSIM
Verify that a current backup has completed
Remove the passcode so border staff can use the phone
Disable encryption to improve battery life abroad
Delete the MDM enrolment to avoid foreign network conflicts
questions.explanation: Travel preparation is about cost and recovery. Sorting out roaming or a local data plan avoids bill shock, and a fresh backup means a lost or damaged phone can be replaced abroad with minimal disruption. Security controls stay in place: the passcode and encryption protect the device if it is lost, and MDM enrolment is what allows the company to locate and wipe it, so none of those should be removed.

distractor_analysis.2: Removing the passcode leaves company data exposed if the phone is lost.
distractor_analysis.3: Encryption has no meaningful battery cost and protects the data.
distractor_analysis.4: Enrolment is what enables remote help and wipe while travelling.

questions.question: Match each mobile network or management term to its description.

pairs.right: Shares the phone's cellular data as a Wi-Fi network
Turns off all wireless radios with one switch
Carrier profile stored on a chip inside the phone
Central platform that enforces policy on enrolled devices
Routes voice calls through an internet connection

questions.explanation: These terms come up constantly in mobile support. A hotspot shares connectivity outward, airplane mode is the master radio switch, an eSIM replaces the plastic card with a programmable profile, MDM is how organisations control fleets of phones, and Wi-Fi calling rescues voice service where the cellular signal is poor. Being able to name the right feature for a user's situation is most of the job.

questions.question: Order the steps an administrator should take when an enrolled corporate phone is reported lost.
sequence: Confirm the report and identify the device record in the management console
Use remote locate to see the last known position and try to contact the finder if appropriate
Lock the device remotely with a message and contact number displayed on the screen
If the device is not recovered within the agreed time, issue a remote wipe
Record the incident, retire the device record and provision a replacement from backup
questions.explanation: The order protects data without destroying recovery chances. Verifying the report avoids wiping a phone that is in a desk drawer. Locating and locking come before wiping because a locked, encrypted phone is already safe from casual access and may still be returned. A wipe is the final step because it is irreversible. Closing the record and restoring the user from backup completes the process and keeps the asset register accurate.

questions.question: A user says the phone's mobile data works but only very slowly on the last day of every month, then recovers. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The plan's high-speed data allowance is used up and the carrier throttles speed until the cycle resets
The SIM card wears out toward the end of the month
The phone's battery is weaker at month end
Cellular towers shut down for maintenance monthly
questions.explanation: Most plans include a monthly allowance of full-speed data. Once it is consumed the carrier reduces the connection to a low speed rather than cutting it off, and the pattern of slowness that resets on the billing date is the tell-tale sign. The fix is a larger plan, using Wi-Fi more, or checking which apps consume the most data in the phone's usage screen. SIMs do not wear, battery state does not throttle data, and towers do not have a monthly outage.

distractor_analysis.1: A SIM is a passive chip with no monthly cycle.
distractor_analysis.2: Battery level does not affect data speed.
distractor_analysis.3: Carriers do not take networks down on a monthly schedule.
